sections.title: The Blessing over Bread
sections.html:
Bread is made from the five species of grain, and therefore seemingly one should have recited over it "who creates the fruit of the ground" (Borei Pri Ha-adama), as one recites over all the species that grow from the ground. However, because of its great importance, being the main food of a person, the Sages instituted a special blessing for it: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth."

Bread is a special food, for all the animals in the world eat natural foods such as grasses, leaves, seeds, grains, vegetables, fruits and even meat, whereas man eats bread, which is a food produced through a lengthy process. Many perceive bread as a natural food and do not notice that it is a food whose preparation requires very many labors: plowing the ground, sowing the wheat, reaping the stalks, separating the kernels of grain from the stalks and the chaff by threshing, winnowing and sorting, grinding the kernels into flour, kneading it with water, and baking the dough into bread. One should further know that the labor of baking is more complex and sophisticated than the labor of cooking, and consequently it expresses more the unique ability of man to prepare his food (see below 6:10, regarding the law of a cooked dish whose level is lower than that of a baked good).

As with bread, so with man: all the animals in the world learn in a short time and in a natural way how to walk, how to obtain their food and how to be fruitful and multiply, whereas man needs many years to learn to obtain food for himself, clothing, shelter from cold and heat, and to establish a family. He must learn everything, but after he has learned and contemplated, he is able to harness the enormous forces of nature to his service: to build houses from stones and earth, to heat them with wood and oil; to sow fields and plant trees, to produce food in abundance and manufacture various garments; to pave roads, to manufacture cars, ships and airplanes, in order to transport people and goods in them.

Animals hardly need to learn how to communicate with members of their species, whereas man needs many years in order to learn to speak, to understand facial expressions and the various emotions, but after he has learned this, his relationships with his family members and friends will be full of endless meaning. Animals have no moral questions about their lives and about the nature around them; they fit in. Whereas man hesitates, asks and struggles, years upon years, generations upon generations, and through this he is able to grasp abstract concepts of good and evil, truth and falsehood, faith and destiny.

One can say that all the animals in the world, together with the fact that they have no free choice and have no ability to create things in the world, also eat simple foods as they are in nature. But man, who has understanding and choice, and on whom rests the responsibility to repair the world, his food too is created through a long process that requires understanding. Therefore it is specifically bread that sustains the heart of man, as it is stated (Tehillim 104:15): "and bread that sustains the heart of man."

Seemingly, after man has toiled so much in preparing the bread, he could become proud and think as if he alone brought forth the bread from the earth. In order that we not err in this, the Sages instituted the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth." For in truth, all the special qualities in the five species of grain and in the earth, as well as our understanding and our ability to make bread, all come from Him, may He be blessed, and therefore in truth it is He who brought forth the bread from the earth. And when a person forgets the One who spoke and the world came into being, he is gradually drawn after his lowly sides, after his evil desires. Then all his great talents become a stumbling block for him, and he uses all his great enterprises to do evil, to destroy and to devastate. Instead of adding life and blessing, he causes death and decay. Only if he remembers the Lord his God, and the wondrous destiny placed upon him, will he be able to direct all his talents for the good, to add life to the world, and to be a partner with God in its repair and its building.

Therefore the blessing over bread is so important, for it connects the food, in which human creative power is expressed, to its Divine source. And by virtue of the blessing, eating bread gives us strength to understand and to comprehend, to keep and to do, all the words of the Torah.

sections.title: Enhancements in the Blessing over Bread
sections.html:
When a person comes to recite a blessing over a food, it is proper that he hold it in his right hand, for thereby the blessing will be said with concentration and respect (as explained below 9:4). And when he comes to recite the blessing over bread, because of its special importance, it is proper that he hold it during the blessing with both hands and with all ten fingers, to allude to the ten mitzvot involved in making bread (SA 167:4; MB 24).

As is known, the more important and vital a matter we are engaged in, the more one can rise through it or, Heaven forbid, fall. And so that we will rise and not fall, the Torah gave us mitzvot to guide us. And the more important the matter, the more mitzvot there are concerning it. Therefore many mitzvot accompany married life and the service of the Holy Temple. And so too regarding the food that sustains a person, and especially bread, for many mitzvot accompany the process of its preparation: 1) When plowing, we were commanded not to plow with an ox and a donkey together. 2) When sowing, we were commanded not to sow kil'ayim (forbidden mixtures). 3) When reaping, we were commanded to leave leket, shikh'ḥa and pe'a (gleanings, forgotten sheaves and the corner of the field) for the poor. 4) When threshing with the help of an animal, we were commanded not to cause it suffering by muzzling its mouth so that it cannot eat. 5) The first fruit of the new grain we were commanded to bring as bikkurim (first fruits) to the kohanim in the Temple. 6) After reaping the wheat, we were commanded to separate teruma and terumat ma'aser for the kohanim; 7) ma'aser rishon (first tithe) for the Levites; 8) ma'aser sheni (second tithe), which must be eaten in sanctity in Jerusalem (in years 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the shemita cycle); 9) and ma'aser ani (the tithe for the poor) for the poor (in years 3 and 6).
10) When kneading the dough, we were commanded to separate ḥalla for the kohen.

One who intends to eat from two kinds of bread should recite the blessing over the more important bread. This is the law for all blessings over enjoyment: if he had, for example, two apples, it is preferable that he say the blessing over the better of them, for in this way the blessing will express the praise in the best way. All the more so is it proper to act this way with bread, and therefore many detailed laws were stated regarding the order of importance and precedence among the various kinds of bread, and the laws of precedence for other foods were learned from it (below 9:9).

This is the order of importance: wheat bread precedes barley bread, because it comes first in the order of the seven species, and also its taste is finer.

One who wishes to eat from a small whole roll and from a large loaf of bread that has already begun to be sliced should preferably recite the blessing over the roll, because it is whole whereas the loaf has already been cut, and the advantage of wholeness takes precedence over the advantage of size.

One who wishes to eat whole-wheat bread and also bread from sifted (white) flour: in the past the ruling was to recite the blessing over the bread from sifted flour, which was considered better. However, today many consider whole-wheat bread to be better. Therefore, one who prefers whole-wheat bread should recite the blessing over it. And one who does not prefer either of them should recite the blessing over the bread from sifted flour.

When there are two breads of equal value, and one is larger than the other, it is preferable to recite the blessing over the larger one, because it is more important (SA 168:1-4; MB 15; SA 211:1-2; MB 33).1

sections.title: Breaking the Bread, and Not Interrupting Between the Blessing and Eating
sections.html:
Since a whole bread is more honored, it is proper to recite the blessing over it while it is still whole. But on the other hand, it is right to attach the Ha-motzi blessing to the eating, and if we recite the blessing over a whole bread we will be forced to delay after the blessing until it is cut. Therefore the Sages said that before the blessing one should begin to cut the bread, in such a way that it still remains attached, so that if he holds it by the small part he can lift all of it. In this state the bread is still considered whole, and at the same time, immediately after the blessing he will be able to finish breaking it and taste from it.

All this refers to bread whose cutting takes some time, but one who comes to eat a roll or a pita, which is easily and quickly broken, should not begin to break it before the blessing, but only after it (SA 167:1, and BHL s.v. "ve-tzarikh").

On Shabbat one should not begin to cut the ḥalla before the blessing, because on Shabbat there is a mitzva to recite the blessing specifically over two whole ḥallot, and if he begins to cut, the ḥalla will no longer be whole (see Rema 167:1; many wrote that one should mark the place of breaking: Baḥ, Maharshal, MB 274:5).

One should break the bread at a place where it is well baked, so that the praise of the blessing will apply to the choicest place in the bread. Today breads are baked uniformly, and one may break at any place in the bread (SA 167:1).2

Immediately after the blessing one should eat from the bread. And if he transgressed and spoke, even one word, before he began to eat, since he interrupted with speech, he has lost the blessing and must recite the blessing again in order to eat. But if he transgressed and spoke after he had put the food into his mouth, he should not recite Ha-motzi again (see below 9:3).

One who speaks between the blessing and eating about a subject related to the food, for example, he recited the blessing over the bread and asked that salt or a knife be brought to him, or asked that bread be brought for a guest, although he acted improperly, since his speech was about a subject related to the eating, this speech does not interpose between the blessing and the eating, and he does not need to recite the blessing again (SA OḤ 167:6).

It is good to eat a kezayit immediately after the blessing without interrupting, in order to give honor to the Ha-motzi blessing. However, when there is a need, one may speak immediately after swallowing a little of the bread.3

sections.title: When Is It Good for One Person to Fulfill the Obligation of His Companions with the Ha-motzi Blessing?
sections.html:
Two people who came to eat bread together, since they have set themselves to eat together, it is good that one recite the blessing aloud and exempt his companion, because a blessing said on behalf of two people is more honorable. And since the listener fulfills his obligation with the blessing he hears from his companion, he may not interrupt with speech until he himself eats.4 But if each one is eating for himself, and they are not waiting for each other, each one must recite the blessing for himself (SA 167:11; see below 5:2).

Accordingly, it is understood why on Shabbatot, when the whole family eats together, they wait until everyone has finished washing their hands, and then the head of the household recites Ha-motzi aloud, and those seated answer "Amen" after him and fulfill their obligation through his blessing. For since they have set themselves to eat together, the enhanced practice is that one person recite Ha-motzi for all. And each of those seated must be careful not to speak until he himself eats.

At a meal with many participants, even though everyone gathered to eat together, it is preferable that at each table one person recite the blessing for his companions who washed their hands with him, because if they wait for all the participants, too great an interruption will be created between the washing and the blessing.5

sections.title: Whether One Must Dip the Bread in Salt
sections.html:
In the past people were accustomed to bake bread without salt, and during the meal they would season the bread with salt, salad or another food. Therefore the Sages said that after the Ha-motzi blessing it is proper to eat the bread in the choicest manner, and thereby emphasize the praise of the blessing; therefore people were accustomed to flavor the bread eaten after the blessing with salt or another food. And one who wished to eat the bread as it is, dry, without salt and other foods, did not need to dip the bread in salt.

Today our breads are baked with salt and spices, so it turns out that our bread is considered choice, and according to the law one may recite the blessing over it as it is, without flavoring it with a little salt or salad (SA 167:5). Nevertheless, many are accustomed to the enhancement of dipping the bread in salt or salad, so that the eating after the blessing will be in the choicest manner.

There is a further enhancement: to place salt on the table during the meal, like the mitzva in the Temple to add salt to the sacrifices, as it is stated (Vayikra 2:13): "With all your offerings you shall offer salt." And we thereby allude that the table is like the altar, and the food like a sacrifice, for it gives a person strength for the service of God (Rema, ibid.).

Some are accustomed, according to Kabbala, to dip the bread in salt (Magen Avraham 167:15; MB 33). The reason for this is that bread alludes to the attribute of ḥesed (kindness), through which a person is nourished and lives, whereas salty salt alludes to the harsh attribute of din (judgment), which, when dominion is given to it, the world is destroyed. And when we dip the bread in salt, we sweeten the salt by making it secondary to the bread, for then it joins the nourishing kindness in the bread, and instead of harming, it benefits. People are accustomed to be scrupulous about this mainly on Shabbatot and Yamim Tovim.

sections.title: Which Foods and Drinks Require a Blessing During the Meal
sections.html:
Bread is the main food of a person, and so we find with Ya'akov our forefather, when fleeing from Esav, that he prayed for bread, as it is stated (Bereishit 28:20): "And Ya'akov made a vow, saying: If God will be with me and will guard me on this way that I am going, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear." And so we find at the time of the famine in Egypt, when the Egyptians turned to Yosef, they said (Bereishit 47:15): "Give us bread; why should we die before you?" and they were prepared to sell all that they had for bread. And likewise when Yosef provided for his father's household, everything he gave them was called bread, as it is stated (ibid. 12): "And Yosef sustained his father and his brothers and all his father's household with bread, according to the little ones." And likewise it is stated about King Belshatzar, who made a great feast: "made a great feast [lit., bread]" (Daniel 5:1).

Thus all of a person's food is called bread; therefore the Ha-motzi blessing exempts all the foods eaten during the meal, such as meat, fish, potatoes, rice, lentils, cheeses, vegetable salad, cooked salads and the like. And even if he eats them by themselves, without bread, the Ha-motzi blessing exempts them. For the Ha-motzi blessing is not directed only toward the bread and what is actually eaten with it, but toward all the foods meant to satisfy. For the main aim of bread is to satisfy, and therefore everything eaten for the sake of satiation is considered secondary to the bread and is exempted by its blessing. It must be emphasized that in order for the bread to exempt the other foods even when they are eaten by themselves, one must eat a kezayit of bread before eating the other foods by themselves.

However, foods meant for dessert, that is, those foods that a person usually eats because of their good taste and not in order to be satisfied, such as dates, grapes, watermelon and the like, are not exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing. For the Ha-motzi blessing applies only to foods meant for satiation, which are the essence of the meal, but desserts, which are eaten to add good taste, and which people usually eat at the end of meals or between them, are an addition to the meal, and one must recite a separate blessing over them.

Therefore, one who eats tree fruits during his meal recites Ha-etz, and one who eats watermelon recites Ha-adama, and one who eats ice cream or pudding recites Shehakol. All this concerns the first blessing, but one does not need to recite a final blessing over them, because Birkat Ha-mazon exempts all the foods eaten during the meal, whether for satiation or for dessert (SA 177:1).6

Drinks that a person usually drinks during his meal, such as water, juice and alcoholic drinks, are exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing. But wine, because of its importance, is not exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing (below 7:3).

Coffee and tea that people usually drink after the food are considered part of the meal and are exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing. But alcoholic drinks that are drunk after the food are not part of the meal, and one recites a blessing over them.7

sections.title: Details of the Laws of Fruit During the Meal
sections.html:
All fruits and vegetables eaten together with foods meant for satiation, whether raw or cooked, are exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing. This includes prunes cooked with meat, raisins in rice, a sweet stew of prunes and apricots (tzimmes), and carrot salad and Waldorf salad served with the courses meant for satiation. But if a sweet carrot salad or Waldorf salad was served after the meal for dessert, one must recite a first blessing over them. Likewise over compote, that is, fruit cooked with sugar, which is served at the end of the meal, one recites a first blessing.

When grapefruit or melon is served at the beginning of the meal, one must recite a first blessing over them, because they are a kind of dessert served at the beginning of the meal in order to open the meal with a good taste, and they are not an actual part of the meal. But foods served at the beginning of the meal in order to arouse the appetite, such as various pickles, are part of the meal, and the Ha-motzi blessing exempts them.

One who intends that one of the courses meant for satiation will consist of fruit, for example grapes: as long as he eats them together with the bread, the grapes are secondary to the bread, and the blessing over the bread exempts them. But if he intends to eat the grapes also by themselves, without bread, there is a doubt whether he will need to recite a blessing over them. In order to avoid the doubt, it is preferable that right at the outset he eat grapes by themselves, and then according to all opinions he recites Ha-etz over them (MB 177:10).8

sections.title: The Law of Cakes and Mezonot During the Meal
sections.html:
Three opinions were stated regarding eating Mezonot baked goods that are meant for dessert during the meal. Some say that one does not recite Mezonot over them, since they resemble bread and they too are satiating, and consequently they are part of the meal and are exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing (Rashba). On the other hand, some say that since they are eaten for dessert and not for satiation, they are not part of the meal, and therefore the Ha-motzi blessing does not exempt them and one must recite Mezonot over them (Tosafot). And some say that the matter is in doubt, and since in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient, one who eats them during the meal should not recite a blessing (see SA 168:7). Those who wish to be scrupulous and avoid the doubt should preferably refrain from eating Mezonot during the meal (Ḥida).

In practice, those who wish to eat Mezonot during the meal must decide for themselves how they relate to eating them. If they decide that it is part of the meal, they should resolve in their minds that the Ha-motzi blessing will always exempt all the Mezonot they eat during the meal, and consequently they will not recite Mezonot over them. And if they decide that eating Mezonot is meant for dessert, they should resolve in their minds that the Ha-motzi blessing will never exempt Mezonot, and they will recite Mezonot over them. And as long as they have not decided, because of the doubt they should not recite Mezonot before them, and if they wish to be scrupulous, they should refrain from eating them during the meal.9

Over Mezonot items that are cooked or deep-fried in oil and served for dessert, such as Bissli, since they do not resemble bread, for bread is baked whereas they are cooked, if they are eaten for dessert one recites Mezonot over them. But over sufganiyot (doughnuts) served at the end of the meal for dessert, although they are cooked in oil, one should not recite Mezonot. For some hold that they are exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing, because their dough resembles bread (below 6, note 9). In addition, they are very satiating, and consequently eating them joins the aim of the meal, and all the foods of the meal are exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing. But since there is doubt about this, le-khatḥila it is preferable to eat them outside the meal, and to recite Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya over them.

sections.title: After the Meal
sections.html:
In the days of the Sages there was a custom to end the meal completely, and since they intended to continue sitting together, they would delay reciting Birkat Ha-mazon, and if more foods were served to them, eating them was considered an eating completely separate from the meal, and therefore they would recite a blessing over it before and after. And afterward they would still complete their obligation with Birkat Ha-mazon.

However, today we are not accustomed to end the meal completely before Birkat Ha-mazon. For as long as we have not yet recited Birkat Ha-mazon, there is still a possibility that we will eat from the bread (SA 177:2). Even if they changed the tablecloth, since it is still possible that they will want to eat more of the bread, we are still considered within the meal. Likewise at weddings, when the waiters clear the tables in order to finish their work, the guests do not wish to end the meal until Birkat Ha-mazon, and it is even possible that they may want to eat more of the bread or other foods if they are brought before them. Therefore, in our days there is no law of 'after the meal'. And if foods are served for dessert, one recites a blessing before them and not after them (as explained above, halakhot 6-7).10

sections.title: How Far the Ha-motzi Blessing Is Effective
sections.html:
The Ha-motzi blessing over bread exempts all the foods and drinks that people usually eat during a meal. And even if the meal continues for many hours, the Ha-motzi blessing recited at the outset exempts all the foods eaten during the meal.

One who decided definitively to end his meal, and then changed his mind and wanted to eat more, the poskim disagreed whether he must recite a blessing before he continues eating. In order to avoid the doubt, it is right that he refrain from continuing to eat. And if after Birkat Ha-mazon he wishes to eat and drink, he should recite blessings before and after them.11

If he has already washed his hands for mayim aḥaronim (the final waters), he is considered as one who has begun Birkat Ha-mazon, and even if he changes his mind and wishes to eat more, he should first recite Birkat Ha-mazon, and if he afterward wishes to eat and drink, he should recite blessings before and after them (SA 179:1).12

A guest who thought that the meal had ended and had already made up his mind not to eat any more, and afterward more foods were brought to him, since he relies on the decision of the host, according to all opinions he may continue eating without reciting a blessing. And the same applies to a man who relies on his wife in matters of food, and likewise those who eat in a dining hall, who rely on the kitchen managers. But if the guest made up his mind that even if more foods were brought to him he would not eat any more of them, and afterward he changed his mind and wanted to eat more, it is right that he refrain from eating and drinking, and rather recite Birkat Ha-mazon (SA 179:2).

One who interrupted in the middle of his meal to pray does not need to recite a blessing again when he returns to eat, because he did not divert his attention from continuing to eat (SA 178:6). One who dozed during his meal, even for an hour, this is not considered an interruption, and when he continues eating he should not recite a blessing again. But if he went to sleep a regular sleep on his bed for more than half an hour, this is like one who diverted his attention from eating, and when he returns to eat he will need to wash his hands with a blessing and recite a blessing before eating (SA 178:7; MB 48; and see above 2:16, note 11).

One who intended to eat from the foods he had at home, and friends came in the middle of the meal and brought him additional foods, or after he finished what he had at home he changed his mind and asked that additional foods be brought to him from the store or from the neighbors, must recite a blessing over those foods, because he certainly did not have them in mind when he recited Ha-motzi (MB 174:18).

sections.title: Whether One May Leave the House in the Middle of the Meal
sections.html:
Le-khatḥila one should not leave the house in the middle of the meal, because some hold that whoever leaves his house has interrupted his meal, and if he wishes to continue eating, he must first recite Birkat Ha-mazon over what he ate, and afterward Ha-motzi over what he intends to eat (Rambam; SA 178:2). However, be-di'avad, if he left his house in the middle of his meal after already having eaten a kezayit of bread, he may continue his meal without reciting Ha-motzi, for be-di'avad we rely on the opinion of those who hold that leaving the house is not considered an interruption for a bread meal. The same applies to one who needed to go out in the middle of his meal for the sake of a mitzva or for another urgent need: if it is clear to him that afterward he will return to continue his meal, he may go out without reciting Birkat Ha-mazon, and when he returns he should continue his meal without reciting Ha-motzi, and when he finishes he should recite Birkat Ha-mazon (Rosh; Rema 178:2). But if when he left the house he completely diverted his attention from the meal, for example he did not intend to continue the meal and also remained outside the place of the meal for more than an hour, if he wishes to continue eating, he will need to wash his hands and recite Ha-motzi (SA 170:1; MB 9).13

If one of the diners remains in the house until the end of the meal, according to all opinions the other participants may leave the house in the middle of the meal when there is a need. And when they return to the meal, according to all opinions they will not need to recite Ha-motzi again, because the one who remained in the house at the place of the meal continues the continuity of the meal on behalf of those who went out (SA 178:2).

Travelers: the entire road is their place, and therefore they may begin eating in one place and continue eating on their way, and the blessing they recited at the outset is effective for them for the continuation of the journey (SA 178:4).

When there is a need, a person may intend, with the Ha-motzi blessing, to begin his meal in one place and continue it afterward in another place. This is what people do when they wish to join a Sheva Berakhot meal after the meal, or when they wish to end the meal at a gathering of friends.14

sections.title: Foods Eaten Before the Meal
sections.html:
One who wishes to eat a meal with bread should not eat or drink beforehand; rather, he should wash his hands and recite Ha-motzi, and afterward eat and drink everything he wishes. For if he eats or drinks before the meal, many times he causes an unnecessary blessing: if he could exempt what he wishes to eat with the Ha-motzi blessing, then by beginning to eat beforehand he caused himself to recite an additional blessing needlessly. Furthermore, after he eats and drinks he will enter into a doubt regarding the final blessing. For it is possible that he must recite a final blessing over what he ate before the meal, and on the other hand, perhaps it is better that he not recite a final blessing, since the Birkat Ha-mazon after the meal will also exempt what he ate before the meal.

And if he is compelled to wait a little until the meal, and in the meantime he wishes to eat or drink something, in order to avoid the doubt he must make a break of half an hour, or at least about a quarter of an hour, between finishing his eating and the beginning of the meal, and in this way, according to all opinions, he should recite a final blessing over what he ate or drank before the meal. Another option: after he eats what he wanted before the meal, he should recite a final blessing, and go outside for a very short walk, in order to create an interruption between his eating before the meal and the meal. This is how one should act at weddings where refreshments are served before the ḥuppa: they should recite a first and final blessing over the refreshments, and afterward the ḥuppa will be an interruption between the refreshments and the meal. Likewise at a brit mila, sometimes people first eat Mezonot and drink soft drinks, and afterward they wish to begin the meal; the right thing is that they make an interruption between eating the refreshments and the meal, and if it is not possible to wait about a quarter of an hour between them, it is good that they go out for a very short walk.

One who began to eat and drink and needs to begin the meal immediately, and cannot go out for a very short walk or wait a quarter of an hour, must know all the details of the laws explained in the note.15
